title: Cannabis Use Across Age Groups in Canada
text:
Cannabis use in Canada is often described as especially common among younger people, but age differences may depend on what aspect of use is being considered. Using the 2025 Canadian Substance Use Survey, this story compares three related behaviours across age groups: any cannabis use in the past year, daily or almost-daily use among people who used cannabis in the past year, and overlapping alcohol–cannabis use among people who used both substances.
The first figure shows a clear age gradient in past-year cannabis use. Weighted prevalence is about 45% among people aged 15–24 and 25–34, then declines steadily to about 17% among adults aged 65 and older. However, the second figure complicates this pattern. Among people who used cannabis in the past year, the proportion using it daily or almost daily changes much less across age groups, remaining roughly one-quarter across the age range.
The strongest age difference appears for overlapping alcohol and cannabis use. Among people who used both substances, about 69% of those aged 15–24 reported using them close enough together for their effects to overlap, compared with about 32% of adults aged 65 and older. Age therefore appears more strongly related to whether cannabis is used, and whether it is combined with alcohol, than to daily use among cannabis users.

title: Cannabis Use Across Age Groups in Canada
section: Past-year cannabis use decreases with age
text:
Past-year cannabis use decreases with age
The first analysis estimates the weighted percentage of respondents in each age group who reported cannabis use in the past 12 months. The survey weight (WGT_PUMF) is used for all point estimates.








Figure 1: Weighted prevalence of cannabis use in the past 12 months by age group. Numbers under age groups are unweighted valid sample sizes.





Past-year cannabis use is highest among respondents aged 15–24 (44.6%) and 25–34 (44.2%). Prevalence then declines across each older age group, reaching 16.7% among adults aged 65 and older.

title: Cannabis Use Across Age Groups in Canada
section: Daily use among cannabis users is comparatively stable
text:
Daily use among cannabis users is comparatively stable
The second analysis changes the denominator. Rather than asking who used cannabis at all, it examines only respondents who reported cannabis use in the past 12 months and asks what proportion used cannabis every day or almost every day.








Figure 2: Weighted percentage reporting daily or almost-daily cannabis use among respondents who used cannabis in the past 12 months. Numbers under age groups are unweighted eligible sample sizes.





The age gradient is much smaller once the analysis is restricted to cannabis users. Daily or almost-daily use ranges from 28.8% among 15–24-year-old users to 24.1% among users aged 65 and older. This suggests that age differences in cannabis involvement are driven more strongly by the likelihood of using cannabis at all than by daily use among people who already use it.

title: Cannabis Use Across Age Groups in Canada
section: Overlapping alcohol and cannabis use shows a stronger age gradient
text:
Overlapping alcohol and cannabis use shows a stronger age gradient
The final analysis examines respondents who used both alcohol and cannabis in the past 12 months. It estimates the percentage who reported using the two substances at the same time, or close enough together for their effects to overlap.








Figure 3: Weighted percentage reporting overlapping alcohol and cannabis use among respondents who used both substances in the past 12 months. Numbers under age groups are unweighted eligible sample sizes.





Overlapping use declines from 69.0% among 15–24-year-old dual users to 31.6% among dual users aged 65 and older. Compared with the relatively modest age differences in daily cannabis use among users, this pattern suggests that age is especially relevant to the context in which cannabis is used, including whether it is combined with alcohol.

title: Cannabis Use Across Age Groups in Canada
section: Cannabis use is common among younger Canadians, then falls with age
text:
Cannabis use is common among younger Canadians, then falls with age
The overall pattern is striking: cannabis use in the past year is common among people under 35, but becomes progressively less common in older age groups. Hover over the bars to see the weighted estimate and sample size.








Figure 4




At first glance, this could make cannabis use look primarily like a younger-person behaviour. But the next figure changes the question from “Who uses cannabis?” to “Among people who use it, how often do they use it?”

title: Cannabis Use Across Age Groups in Canada
section: Among cannabis users, daily use looks much more similar across ages
text:
Among cannabis users, daily use looks much more similar across ages








Figure 5




Roughly one in four past-year cannabis users in every age group reported daily or almost-daily use. The difference between the youngest and oldest users is much smaller than the difference in whether they used cannabis at all.

title: Cannabis Use Across Age Groups in Canada
section: What changes most with age is combining cannabis with alcohol
text:
What changes most with age is combining cannabis with alcohol








Figure 6




Among people who used both alcohol and cannabis in the past year, nearly 7 in 10 people aged 15–24 reported overlapping use. That proportion falls steadily with age and is closer to 3 in 10 among adults aged 65 and older. The broader story is therefore not simply that cannabis use declines with age. Age differences are especially pronounced in whether cannabis is used at all and whether it is combined with alcohol, while daily use among cannabis users is comparatively similar across age groups.
